export const meta = {
  name: 'visca-gap-reconstruction',
  description: 'Harvest the Crestron VISCA command reference and test whether it can reconstruct the IL-only transformations, calibrated against declared ones',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Harvest', detail: 'scrape the Crestron NextGen Cameras VISCA command reference' },
    { title: 'Experiment', detail: 'control group on 27 declared transformations; reconstruct the 6 IL-only ones; coverage delta' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial check per dimension' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'can documentation close a known compiled-code gap?' },
  ],
}

const R = '/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert'
const DOC = 'https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/9440/Content/Topics/NextGenCameras/Configuration/VISCA-Commands.htm'

const GROUND = `
PROJECT: ${R} — converting AV control-system device drivers between vendors.

THE EXPERIMENT YOU ARE RUNNING, and why it is designed this way.

Crestron's 1 Beyond IV-CAM-I20 and IV-CAM-P20 IP drivers are SDK V2 (Entity Model) .NET
assemblies whose behaviour is ALMOST fully declarative: a large embedded JSON
(116,874 B for I20, 109,648 B for P20, SchemaVersion 2.0) carrying Commands, Responses,
Conditions, Transformations, Rules, Controllers and a DriverController section.

But a handful of Transformations that the JSON's own Rules INVOKE have no definition in the
JSON's Transformations array. Their behaviour exists only as compiled IL registered via
[ImplementationProviderAttribute]:

  P20 driver-local IL:  FormatRomVersion, ParseDecimal, ZoomLevelToPosition,
                        ZoomPositionToLevel, ApplyZoomPositionStep,
                        plus OverridePolynomial (an override hook never called by literal name)
  I20:                  the same family PLUS ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles

(P20 references 39 distinct Transformation names; 27 are declared in the JSON; of the 12
undeclared only those ~5-6 have driver-local IL — the rest are supplied by the SDK framework.)

Earlier project work established that vendor DOCUMENTATION cannot generate a whole driver: for
the Automate VX, Extron's working driver calls 5 endpoints with no trace in the docs at all,
including Wake (while Sleep IS documented), and sends three parameters with JSON types the spec
contradicts. See findings/08.

THIS EXPERIMENT ASKS A DIFFERENT AND BETTER-POSED QUESTION: documentation may be unable to
generate a whole driver, but can it FILL PRECISELY-KNOWN, ALREADY-ENUMERATED HOLES?

The repo owner supplied Crestron's VISCA command reference for these cameras:
  ${DOC}

The cameras demonstrably speak VISCA: the I20 driver JSON mentions 'Visca' 121 times and 'Nibble'
40 times, and DECLARES transformations including ViscaAddressToHeader, MapBooleanToViscaOnOff,
PanTiltAngleToPosition, PanTiltPositionToAngle, ZoomPositionToFieldOfView, FieldOfViewToZoomPosition,
MapPanDirection, MapTiltDirection, MapZoomSpeedZoomDirection, MapExposureMode, MapFocusMode,
MapAutoFocusBehavior, MapModelCodeToModel, MapTrackingFramingProfileToPreset, AsByte,
FromBytesToUInt, FromBytesToInt, RoundToInt, RoundToTenths, InvertBoolean and others.

THE CRITICAL METHODOLOGICAL DEVICE — a control group:
The 27 DECLARED transformations have their definitions visible IN THE JSON. So they are a
CALIBRATION SET. If the VISCA documentation correctly predicts what the declared transformations
do, it has earned trust for the undeclared ones. If it cannot even predict the declared ones,
we learn that cheaply and stop. Do not skip this step and jump to the interesting part.

TOOLS AVAILABLE:
- Extract any Crestron package: 'python3 ${R}/tools/pkg_dump.py <path.pkg>' or import pkg_dump and
  call process_pkg(path) -> dict with 'driver_definition'.
- Packages:
  "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-i12_i20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.pkg"
  "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-p12_p20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-P20_IP.pkg"

RULES:
- Web access ONLY via the Bright Data CLI: 'brightdata scrape <url>' / 'brightdata search "q"'.
  Never WebFetch/WebSearch, never curl to target sites — the owner's home IP must not be used.
- Cite a URL, a JSON path, or a byte offset for EVERY claim. No citation, no finding.
- NEVER submit placeholder or test content. An honest gap beats a stub.
- DO NOT decompile or disassemble the driver IL to answer these questions. Crestron's SDK licence
  section 4.2(c) bars discovering underlying ideas or algorithms by reverse engineering,
  de-compilation or disassembly, and the entire point of this experiment is to establish whether
  the DOCUMENTED route reaches the same answer. Reading metadata that pkg_dump already surfaces
  (type and method NAMES, attribute registrations) is fine — that is not decompilation. Reading IL
  method BODIES is not.
- Structured output must be valid JSON: no angle brackets, no XML-ish tags, no unescaped
  backslashes, no raw newlines inside strings.
- FILE WRITES: only the harvest agent writes, and only under ${R}/reference/crestron-visca/.
  Nobody writes under ${R}/tools/. Everyone else uses /tmp.
`

const FIND = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          evidence: { type: 'string' },
          confidence: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          implication: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'evidence', 'confidence'],
      },
    },
    openQuestions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'summary', 'findings'],
}

const VERD = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    verified: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['CONFIRMED', 'REFUTED', 'UNCERTAIN', 'OVERSTATED'] },
          note: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'verdict'],
      },
    },
    missedOrWrong: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'verified'],
}

phase('Harvest')
log('Harvesting the Crestron NextGen Cameras VISCA command reference')

const harvest = await agent(
  `${GROUND}\n\nYOUR TASK: harvest Crestron's VISCA command reference for these cameras and save it
into the repo. You are the ONLY agent permitted to write files, and only under
${R}/reference/crestron-visca/.

Start at ${DOC}. That page is part of a larger "NextGen Cameras" documentation set (docs.crestron.com
area 9440) — follow its siblings too: anything covering camera configuration, PTZ, zoom, presets,
the command protocol, IP/serial control setup, and any page listing supported models (establish
whether IV-CAM-I20 and IV-CAM-P20 are in scope for this doc, and SAY SO — if these pages cover a
different camera family the whole experiment is weakened and that must be reported, not glossed).

Save each page as markdown under ${R}/reference/crestron-visca/, each beginning with a
'Source: <url>' line. Write an INDEX.md listing every page with its URL.

Most importantly write COMMANDS.md tabulating every VISCA command documented: command name, the
byte sequence with its parameter positions marked, parameter ranges and units, the expected reply,
and any notes on encoding. VISCA conventionally encodes multi-byte values as sequences of bytes
each carrying 4 significant bits (low nibbles) — capture EXACTLY how this documentation expresses
that, verbatim, including any worked example, because it is the crux of the experiment.

Also capture anything about zoom: position ranges, zoom level vs zoom position, optical/digital
boundaries, field-of-view relationships, step behaviour, and any conversion table or formula.

Report: pages fetched, commands documented, whether the doc covers the I20/P20 models specifically,
and anything you could not reach. Do not fabricate a command.`,
  { label: 'harvest:visca-docs', phase: 'Harvest', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
)

const DIMS = [
  {
    key: 'control-group',
    prompt: `RUN THE CALIBRATION. This decides whether the rest of the experiment means anything,
so do it rigorously and report the result honestly even if it is discouraging.

Take the 27 transformations DECLARED in the I20 driver JSON (extract with pkg_dump; they are in the
'Transformations' array, each with a Name, a Type and an Info block that defines its behaviour).

For EACH declared transformation, ask: could this definition have been PREDICTED from the harvested
VISCA documentation at ${R}/reference/crestron-visca/ alone, by someone who had not seen the JSON?

Score each one: FULLY PREDICTABLE / PARTIALLY / NOT PREDICTABLE, with the specific doc evidence (or
its absence) that justifies the score. Be strict — "the doc mentions pan/tilt so I could have
guessed PanTiltAngleToPosition" is NOT prediction. Prediction means the doc supplies the actual
numbers, ranges, mappings or formulas the JSON encodes.

Pay particular attention to the ones that should be most doc-determined:
ViscaAddressToHeader (VISCA addressing is protocol-standard), MapBooleanToViscaOnOff (the on/off
byte values), AsByte / FromBytesToUInt / FromBytesToInt (encoding primitives),
PanTiltAngleToPosition and PanTiltPositionToAngle (need real position ranges),
ZoomPositionToFieldOfView and FieldOfViewToZoomPosition (need a real curve or table).

Produce an overall CALIBRATION SCORE: what fraction of known-answer transformations does this
documentation actually predict? State plainly whether the documentation has earned trust for the
undeclared ones, and note any systematic pattern in what it predicts well versus badly — e.g. if it
nails protocol-level encoding but fails on device-specific curves, that is exactly the shape of
answer the project needs.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'reconstruct-il-gaps',
    prompt: `THE MAIN EVENT. Attempt to RECONSTRUCT, from the harvested documentation plus the
driver's own declarative data, each transformation that exists only as compiled IL:

  ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles  (I20 only)
  ZoomLevelToPosition
  ZoomPositionToLevel
  ApplyZoomPositionStep
  FormatRomVersion
  ParseDecimal

You may NOT decompile the IL — that is the point of the experiment and it is also barred by
Crestron's licence. Work from: the VISCA documentation, the VISCA protocol convention generally,
and crucially the DRIVER'S OWN JSON, which constrains each transformation heavily. The JSON shows
where each is invoked, what Input placeholders feed it, what Output name it produces, and how that
output is consumed by a Command template — so the input and output shapes are pinned even though
the body is not.

For each, produce: a precise natural-language specification, a reference implementation in Python,
and the evidence chain that justifies it. Then TEST your reconstruction against the driver's own
data wherever possible — for example, if ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles feeds a Command template whose
surrounding literal bytes are visible, your implementation must produce a byte sequence consistent
with that template and with any documented example in the VISCA reference. Show the worked check.

Rate each reconstruction: CONFIDENT (doc plus JSON pin it exactly) / PLAUSIBLE (consistent but
under-determined) / FAILED (cannot be pinned down), and say precisely what additional information
would settle any FAILED one.

Be honest about under-determination. A reconstruction that merely looks reasonable and is wrong
would produce a driver that sends subtly incorrect bytes — the worst failure mode in this project.
Prefer PLAUSIBLE over CONFIDENT when the evidence does not fully constrain the answer.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'doc-vs-driver-delta',
    prompt: `Run the doc-versus-driver delta test on the CRESTRON side, as a third data point for a
pattern the project has now seen twice (Samsung: two vendors independently encoded the same
undocumented firmware bug; Automate VX: Extron calls 5 endpoints absent from the vendor docs).

Compare the harvested VISCA command reference against what the I20 and P20 drivers ACTUALLY send.
Extract every Command from both drivers' JSON, resolve its template to a byte pattern, and match it
to a documented VISCA command.

Report:
1. COVERAGE — how many documented VISCA commands does each driver implement? Which does it ignore?
2. EXTRAS — does either driver send commands NOT in the documentation? These are the interesting
   ones. Characterise them: vendor-specific extensions, undocumented registers, tracking/AI
   features unique to the 1 Beyond line?
3. CONTRADICTIONS — anywhere the driver's bytes disagree with the documented bytes. As established
   in findings/05 and 08, where a shipped working driver and a document disagree, the driver is
   evidence of what the hardware does and the document is evidence of intent.
4. I20 vs P20 — do the two drivers' command sets differ in ways the documentation explains
   (different camera capabilities) or does one carry commands the doc attributes only to the other?

State whether the project's standing conclusion — that a shipped driver records what a device does
while documentation records what someone intended, and the delta is the driver's value — REPRODUCES
here, is contradicted, or is untestable on this evidence.`,
  },
]

phase('Experiment')
const done = await pipeline(
  DIMS,
  (d) => agent(`${GROUND}\n\nThe VISCA documentation has been harvested to ${R}/reference/crestron-visca/.\n` +
    `Harvest report:\n${harvest}\n\nYOUR DIMENSION: ${d.key}\n\n${d.prompt}`, {
    label: `exp:${d.key}`, phase: 'Experiment', schema: FIND, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high',
  }),
  (res, d) => {
    if (!res) return null
    return agent(
      `${GROUND}\n\nYou are an adversarial verifier for "${d.key}". REFUTE the findings below rather than ` +
      `agreeing. Reproduce each claim yourself against the harvested docs and the driver JSON.\n\n` +
      `Be most skeptical of RECONSTRUCTIONS: for any transformation the researcher claims to have ` +
      `reconstructed, try to find an alternative implementation equally consistent with the same evidence. ` +
      `If you can, the reconstruction is under-determined and must be downgraded — say so. Also recount any ` +
      `calibration score or coverage percentage yourself.\n\n` +
      `CONFIRMED only if you personally reproduced it. REFUTED if contradicted. OVERSTATED if directionally ` +
      `right but claimed too strongly. UNCERTAIN if uncheckable.\n\n` +
      `If the researcher submitted placeholder or test content, say so explicitly in missedOrWrong.\n\n` +
      `Their brief:\n${d.prompt}\n\nFINDINGS:\n${JSON.stringify(res, null, 2)}`,
      { label: `verify:${d.key}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERD, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
    ).then((v) => ({ dimension: d.key, analysis: res, verification: v }))
  }
)

const dossier = done.filter(Boolean)
const counts = dossier.reduce((a, d) => {
  for (const v of (d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []) a[v.verdict] = (a[v.verdict] || 0) + 1
  return a
}, {})
log(`Experiment done: ${dossier.length}/${DIMS.length} — ${JSON.stringify(counts)}`)

phase('Synthesize')
const synthesis = await agent(
  `${GROUND}\n\nHarvest report and verified dossier follow. Treat REFUTED as false, OVERSTATED as ` +
  `weaker, UNCERTAIN as unproven.\n\nWrite the synthesis. Answer, in order:\n\n` +
  `1. THE HEADLINE: can vendor documentation close a precisely-known compiled-code gap? Lead with the ` +
  `calibration result, because it determines how much the rest is worth. Then give the per-transformation ` +
  `verdict.\n` +
  `2. Which of the six IL-only transformations are now recoverable without decompilation, and which ` +
  `remain out of reach? For the latter, what would settle them?\n` +
  `3. What this means for "Crestron in" on SDK V2 drivers: does the reachable fraction of the catalogue ` +
  `go up, and by how much? Be concrete about what a converter should now do when it meets an undeclared ` +
  `transformation — special-case a known set, consult a doc-derived library, or fail loudly?\n` +
  `4. Did the doc-versus-driver delta pattern reproduce on the Crestron side?\n` +
  `5. What should change in findings 07 and 08, and the single highest-value next step.\n\n` +
  `Be rigorous about uncertainty: a reconstruction that looks right and is wrong would emit subtly ` +
  `incorrect bytes, which is this project's worst failure mode. Say plainly which results are safe to ` +
  `build on and which are not.\n\n` +
  `Prose with headings, minimal bullets, cite evidence, no padding. The reader is an AV professional ` +
  `who writes code.\n\nHARVEST:\n${harvest}\n\nDOSSIER:\n${JSON.stringify(dossier, null, 2)}`,
  { label: 'synthesis:visca', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'opus', effort: 'high' }
)

return { harvest, dimensions: dossier.length, verdictCounts: counts, dossier, synthesis }

result.harvest:
All 14 content pages have a proper `Source:` line, plus COMMANDS.md and INDEX.md as the two synthesis files (16 files total). The harvest is complete and written under the permitted directory.

## Summary

**Pages fetched (16 total, all via Bright Data CLI, none via direct WebFetch/curl):**
- 14 individual doc pages saved as markdown with `Source: <url>` headers, plus `COMMANDS.md` (the tabulated command reference) and `INDEX.md`, all under `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/reference/crestron-visca/`.
- Core protocol pages: VISCA-Commands, VISCA-Lightbar-Commands, VISCA-Intelligent-Switching-Commands, Reserved-Presets.
- Model-scope pages: IV-CAM-P20-Specifications, IV-CAM-I20-Specifications.
- Configuration/PTZ context pages: Camera-Controls, Set-a-Static-IP-Address, Tracking-Menu, Presenter-Tracking-Settings, Intelligent-Switching, Tracking-Settings, Change-the-Camera-Mode, Perform-a-Factory-Restore.
- 4 content-free navigation stubs were fetched but not saved (listed in INDEX.md); several more sibling pages were identified by name via search but not fetched (also listed in INDEX.md as follow-up candidates).

**Scope finding (reported, not glossed over):** the doc set ("IV-CAM Series Manual", docs.crestron.com area 9440) explicitly and repeatedly covers both cameras in question — dedicated per-model spec pages exist for P20 and I20, `CAM_MountMode` and the lightbar page both call out "IV-CAM-P12 and IV-CAM-P20" / "IV-CAM-I12-B and IV-CAM-I20" by name, and Reserved-Presets differentiates I20-specific preset numbers (82/83 Group Tracking, 101-108 Preset Zones/Tracking Profiles). One gap: no P20-specific reserved-preset rows appear anywhere in this doc set.

**Commands documented in `COMMANDS.md`:** the full main Commands table (~19 command sets: AddressSet, IF_Clear, Command Cancel, CAM_Power, CAM_Zoom, CAM_Focus, CAM_ZoomFocus, CAM_WB, CAM_RGain, CAM_BGain, CAM_AE, CAM_Shutter, CAM_Iris, CAM_Gain, CAM_Bright, CAM_ExpComp, CAM_Backlight, CAM_Memory, Freeze, IR_Receive, Pan-tiltDrive, Pan-tiltLimitSet, CAM_MountMode), the full Inquiry Commands table (~20 inquiries), ACK/Completion/Error message formats, the Zoom Ratio/Position tables (12x and 20x lenses), the Exposure Comp table, the full VISCA Lightbar command set (status colors + 18 common combos + the bit-packing procedure with its worked example), and the full VISCA Intelligent Switching command set (8 commands).

**The nibble-encoding crux (Section 1 of COMMANDS.md):** the main VISCA-Commands page expresses multi-byte parameters only *typographically* (`0p 0q 0r 0s` placeholders, one significant nibble per byte, prefixed `0`) — it never narrates the packing rule in prose. The only page with a fully worked, prose-narrated example is VISCA-Lightbar-Commands, but that example turns out to use a *different* bit-packing scheme (2-bit brightness + 2-bit color sub-fields per byte) than the standard "4-bit VISCA value nibble" convention used by zoom/focus/pan-tilt — documented as a useful negative control, not glossed over. I also derived and flagged a worked cross-check: translating a Zoom Ratio table entry (`28F6`) into the `CAM_Zoom Direct` packet's `0p 0q 0r 0s` nibbles requires a translation step (`02 08 0F 06`) that the doc never states outright — exactly the kind of gap the experiment is designed to surface.

**Anomalies flagged (not silently fixed):** the CAM_Zoom "Absolute Position" packet doesn't fit the standard nibble pattern; the Exposure Comp table's third column appears to be a copy-paste leftover from the Zoom Ratio table; VISCA/UDP is named on the spec pages but never mentioned in any VISCA command page's transport prose; the Pan-tiltDrive table's "1 angle=14.4" notes are misaligned to the Down-Left/Down-Right rows rather than the Absolute/Relative Position rows that actually use them.

**Not reached:** several Camera Manager 2 UI sub-pages (OSD menu, Add Cameras, Set the Tracking Zone/Shots, various Intelligent Switching sub-pages, I12/P12 spec pages) were identified by name via search-snippet titles but their exact URLs weren't resolved/fetched — listed explicitly in `INDEX.md` for a follow-up pass. None of these are VISCA byte-level protocol pages, so their absence doesn't affect the COMMANDS.md tabulation.

analysis.summary: Calibration run against all 26 declared Transformations in the I20 driver JSON (pkg_dump of Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.pkg, driver_definition.Transformations). Score: 12 FULLY PREDICTABLE, 5 PARTIALLY, 9 NOT PREDICTABLE — strict fraction fully-predicted = 12/26 (46%); weighted (Full=1, Partial=0.5) = 14.5/26 (56%). The documentation earns CONDITIONAL trust with a sharp, legible pattern: it reliably reproduces protocol-level command-byte conventions that repeat across many rows of the Commands/Inquiry tables (on/off=0x02/0x03, focus/pan/tilt direction codes, exposure-mode codes, zoom-speed codes, the 14.4 pan/tilt scale constant, and reserved-preset-to-hex mapping), but it fails completely on device-specific analog curves and proprietary numeric codes (the zoom-position-to-field-of-view polynomial, the model-code table, AF-behavior submodes) that never appear anywhere in the harvested pages. This is exactly the failure shape the experiment needs to know before trusting the doc on the undeclared transformations: ZoomPositionToFieldOfView/FieldOfViewToZoomPosition (the closest doc analogs to the undeclared ZoomLevelToPosition/ZoomPositionToLevel/ApplyZoomPositionStep family) scored NOT PREDICTABLE, which is a strong negative signal for that part of the experiment specifically.

findings.claim: ViscaAddressToHeader (Math, Add, Operand 128) — PARTIALLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: COMMANDS.md Section 0 states the command header convention '8x, where x is the camera address' and separately states for replies 'z = Device address + 8' (verbatim, cited beneath the Error Messages table, reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md lines 26-29, 122). This supports guessing 'add a constant tied to 8' but the doc never states the operation as byte-level addition of 128, nor resolves whether the '+8' in the reply formula is a nibble-add or byte-add — the two phrasings (a fixed high nibble '8' vs. an explicit '+8' arithmetic note) are not reconciled into one formula anywhere in the doc set.

findings.claim: AsByte / FromBytesToUInt / FromBytesToInt (Math, UIntToBigEndianBytes / BigEndianBytesToUint / BigEndianBytesToInt) — PARTIALLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: COMMANDS.md Section 1 documents two distinct parameter shapes verbatim: single full-range bytes (e.g. CAM_Memory 'pp: Memory Number =0 to 255', line 202) versus 4-nibble split parameters ('0p 0q 0r 0s', lines 43-59) — this distinction matches AsByte's Operand=1 (single byte, no split) versus the nibble-transformation family. Byte order (MSB-first / big-endian) is inferable only by pattern-matching left-to-right placeholder order across every multi-byte table row, exactly as COMMANDS.md Section 1 itself flags ('does not narrate the packing/unpacking algorithm in words anywhere on this page', lines 61-65) — no page states 'big-endian' in prose.

findings.claim: PanTiltAngleToPosition (Multiply, 14.4) and PanTiltPositionToAngle (Divide, 14.4) — FULLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: VISCA-Commands.md lines 582 and 592 (verbatim, and reproduced in COMMANDS.md lines 217-218): 'YYYY: pan absolute position: 1 angle=14.4' and 'ZZZZ: tilt absolute position: 1 angle=14.4'. The exact multiplier 14.4 used in the driver JSON's Info.Operand is present in the doc text, even though the doc misattaches the note to the wrong table rows (Down-Left/Down-Right instead of Absolute/Relative Position).

findings.claim: RoundToInt (Round, no operand) and RoundToTenths (Round, Operand 1) — NOT PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: No page in reference/crestron-visca states a rounding rule or precision for any derived value; the spec pages (IV-CAM-P20-Specifications.md, IV-CAM-I20-Specifications.md) give FOV as 'Horizontal: 56.45°' (2 decimal places), which does not match a 'round to tenths' (1 decimal place) convention. Both transformations are display/serialization implementation choices with zero doc support.

findings.claim: MapBooleanToViscaOnOff (true=0x02, false=0x03) and MapPtzSuperOperationStateToBoolean (0x02=true, 0x03=false) — FULLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: COMMANDS.md main Commands table: CAM_Power On/Off = '...00 02 FF'/'...00 03 FF' (lines 139-140), CAM_ExpComp On/Off = '3E 02 FF'/'3E 03 FF' (194-195), CAM_Backlight On/Off = '33 02 FF'/'33 03 FF' (200-201), IR_Receive On/Off = '06 08 02 FF'/'06 08 03 FF' (209-210) — the 0x02=On/0x03=Off convention repeats across at least 4 independent command families in the same table, giving high-confidence prediction of both the value and its inverse mapping.

findings.claim: MapExposureMode (true=0x00, false=0x03; comment cites 0x0A/0x0B) — FULLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: COMMANDS.md CAM_AE row group (lines 173-177): Full Auto='39 00 FF', Manual='39 03 FF', Shutter Priority='39 0A FF', Iris Priority='39 0B FF' — matches the JSON transformation's own Comment field ('Full Auto = 0x00, Manual = 0x03, Shutter Priority = 0x0a, Iris Priority = 0x0b') exactly, byte for byte.

findings.claim: MapFocusDirection (Farther=0x02, Closer=0x03, default/stop=0x00) and MapFocusMode (true=0x02, false=0x03) — FULLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: COMMANDS.md CAM_Focus rows (lines 148-156): Stop='08 00 FF', Far(Standard)='08 02 FF', Near(Standard)='08 03 FF', Auto Focus='38 02 FF', Manual Focus='38 03 FF' — direct byte match for both transformations.

findings.claim: MapAutoFocusBehavior (global=0x00, center=0x01, face=0x04) — NOT PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: grep across all 16 harvested files for 'face|autofocus|auto focus|AF area|focus area|focus behavior|global|center' finds only Camera-Controls.md's binary AF toggle description ('AF: Use to auto focus the PTZ camera lens... Auto focus is only available when presenter tracking is disabled') and an unrelated mention of face-detection boxes in Presenter Tracking debug mode (line 77) — no page documents an AF area/behavior submode concept, its labels, or any byte codes for it.

findings.claim: MapZoomSpeedZoomDirection (Tele-Std=0x02, Wide-Std=0x03, Tele-variable 0/In..7/In=0x20..0x27, Wide-variable 0/Out..7/Out=0x30..0x37) — FULLY PREDICTABLE
findings.evidence: COMMANDS.md CAM_Zoom rows (lines 142-145): Tele(Standard)='07 02 FF', Wide(Standard)='07 03 FF', Tele(Variable)='07 2p FF, p:0(Low)-7(High)', Wide(Variable)='07 3p FF'. analysis.summary: Reconstructed all six IL-only transformations from the driver JSON's own invocation sites (Rules/Responses/Controllers) plus the harvested VISCA documentation. Two (ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles, ParseDecimal) are CONFIDENT: the JSON pins exact input/output byte shapes and the doc's own Reserved-Presets table plus a second independent worked example (the doc's CAM_Zoom nibble-packing check) let me derive and numerically verify the exact algorithm. Two (ApplyZoomPositionStep, FormatRomVersion) are PLAUSIBLE: role and call sites are pinned exactly by the JSON, but the precise internal algorithm (quantization/step-enforcement rule; version string formatting convention) is genuinely under-determined by any harvested page. Two (ZoomLevelToPosition, ZoomPositionToLevel) are split-rated: PLAUSIBLE for the documented optical range (1x-20x, position 0-16384, interpolated from the doc's own 20x Zoom Ratio table) but FAILED for the undocumented digital-zoom range (20x-320x / position 16384-31424) -- with one important mitigating discovery from the JSON's own control flow: ZoomLevelToPosition's output above 20x is provably dead code (Rule 21 always overrides it with a literal 16384), so only ZoomPositionToLevel's digital-range gap is functionally live (it feeds real device-polled feedback).

findings.claim: ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles(bytes) = (bytes[0]&0x0F)<<4 | (bytes[1]&0x0F) -- packs 2 single-nibble bytes into 1 output byte, high nibble first. Rating: CONFIDENT.
findings.evidence: JSON pin: /tmp/edc/i20.json .Responses[26] 'ViscaTrackingFramingProfileInquiryResponse' -- Match regex '^[\x90-\xf0]P(\x06[\x09-\x0c])\xff' captures 2 bytes as PresetNibbles, ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles(PresetNibbles)->Preset, then MapTrackingFramingProfileToPreset(~{Preset})->TrackingFramingProfile using the DECLARED (calibration-set) map {trackingProfile1:'i'(0x69), trackingProfile2:'j'(0x6a), trackingProfile3:'k'(0x6b), trackingProfile4:'l'(0x6c)}. Computing (0x06<<4|0x09)=0x69, (0x06<<4|0x0a)=0x6a, (0x06<<4|0x0b)=0x6b, (0x06<<4|0x0c)=0x6c reproduces all 4 map values exactly. Cross-checked against reference/crestron-visca/Reserved-Presets.md ('105 Tracking Profile 1' ... '108 Tracking Profile 4'; 0x69=105 ... 0x6c=108). SECOND independent confirmation: the same nibble-assembly algorithm generalized to N=4 bytes (the sibling, framework-supplied transformation ViscaAssemble4LowerNibbles, used 9x in each JSON, e.g. i20.json .Responses[10] for ViscaZoomPositionInquiryResponse) reproduces reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md section 6's own worked check: nibble bytes [02,08,0F,06] -> assembled bytes 28 F6 -> uint 0x28F6=10486, matching the doc's stated '20x Zoom 4x = 28F6' row exactly (COMMANDS.md lines 355-364).
findings.implication: Safe to ship this reconstruction verbatim; both P20 and I20 JSONs use the identical convention (P20 lacks ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles only because it has no TrackingFramingProfile preset feature per Reserved-Presets.md's I20-only rows).

findings.claim: ParseDecimal(s) is a plain string->numeric parse with no rounding or unit change. Rating: CONFIDENT on role/behavior; the exact .NET numeric type (decimal vs double) is unpinnable without IL but functionally irrelevant to a Python port.
findings.evidence: JSON pin: i20.json .Rules[27] 'FeedbackForReportedZoomLevelAndReportedFieldOfView', Transformations[2]: ParseDecimal Input={ZoomPositionPollingOnly} Output={ZoomPositionPollingOnly} (same variable name in and out) -- placed immediately before Transformations[3] ZoomPositionToFieldOfView, a declared Polynomial transformation that requires a numeric InputList arg. ZoomPositionPollingOnly's own origin (i20.json .Responses[10] Transformations[2], an 'Identity' copy from {ZoomPosition}, itself FromBytesToUInt output) is already numeric at creation, so the re-parse step only makes sense as a defensive numeric-type coercion after the value round-trips through this SDK's string-based state/placeholder engine.
findings.implication: A no-op float()/Decimal.Parse() port is safe; no special-casing needed.

findings.claim: ApplyZoomPositionStep(position, model, mode) rounds a computed floating zoom-position to a valid integer device position and (plausibly) enforces a minimum step for relative Increment/Decrement moves; exact quantization/clamp rule is NOT pinned. Rating: PLAUSIBLE.
findings.evidence: JSON pins the call CONTRACT precisely: i20.json .Rules[20-23] and .Controllers[10] (FieldOfView.ToDeviceTransformations[2]) all call ApplyZoomPositionStep(InputList=[computed float position, {Model}, literal 'Set'|'Increment'|'Decrement']). Tracing the surrounding control flow shows every LIVE call site's input position is already bounded to the optical range 0-16384 (Rule 20's own Condition 'ZoomLevelIsLessThanOrEqualToOpticalZoomMax' i20.json .Conditions[17]; Rules 22/23's Condition 'ZoomPositionIsLessThanOpticalZoomMax' i20.json .Conditions[19]; Controller FieldOfView's own Info.Max=16384). Rule 21's call (the only one whose ZoomLevel input can exceed 20x) has its transformation OUTPUT discarded -- Rule 21's States.ZoomPosition is the literal 16384, not {ZoomPositionFromLevel} (i20.json .Rules[21].Info.States). No doc page or JSON field states the exact rounding/step-enforcement algorithm.
findings.implication: A reconstruction that only rounds-and-clamps to [0,16384] will be functionally correct for every call site actually exercised in this driver; a wrong guess about minimum-step enforcement for Increment/Decrement could only ever cause a stuck-zoom UX bug, not an out-of-range byte on the wire, since Rule 20/22/23's own Conditions already gate the range.

findings.claim: FormatRomVersion(2 bytes) -> firmware version string; exact string format (e.g. '{major}.{minor:02d}') is a plausible best guess, not verified. Rating: PLAUSIBLE.
findings.evidence: JSON pin: i20.json .Responses[19]/p20.json .Responses[20] 'ViscaVersionInquiryResponse' Select.RomVersion captures exactly 2 raw bytes at the position documented in reference/crestron-visca/VISCA-Commands.md line 850 ('r,s,t,u: ROM version' inside CAM_VersionInq's 'y0 50 00 01 mn pq rs tu vw FF' reply). Output DeviceFirmwareVersion is typed as a bare 'string' with no format constraint anywhere in DriverController.Features[0].EntityModel.Properties['deviceInformation:firmwareVersion'] (Definition.typeDef={'type':'string'}). No page in reference/crestron-visca gives a worked real ROM-version example. A brightdata search of the wider VISCA ecosystem (non-Crestron) turned up only an analogous-but-different Aver PTZ command whose doc states a dotted nibble-digit format ('...FF fw_ver: p.q...') for a DIFFERENT command byte (0x36 0x69, not CAM_VersionInq's 0x00 0x02) -- circumstantial support for a dotted-decimal convention in this protocol family, not proof for this exact field.
findings.implication: Do not trust the exact separator/digit-count/padding without either (a) capturing a live device's real VersionInq reply against its known firmware label, or (b) finding the specific Crestron/1-Beyond doc that states the ROM-version display convention. This is the cleanest 'settle by getting more information' gap in the set.

findings.claim: ZoomLevelToPosition/ZoomPositionToLevel implement a model-dependent, non-linear ZoomLevel<->ZoomPosition curve; PLAUSIBLE (interpolated from the doc's 20-point table) for the optical range 1x-20x / position 0-16384, but FAILED (zero documentation of any kind) for the digital-zoom range 20x-320x / position 16384-31424.
findings.evidence: JSON pins the exact numeric bounds: i20.json Controllers named 'ZoomLevel' (Info.Min=1.0, Max=320.0, Step=0.1) and 'ZoomPosition' (Info.Min=0, Max=31424, Step=1); Rules[31] 'FeedbackForZoomAndFocusRanges20' (Condition ModelIsP20OrI20) sets ZoomLevel.Max=320.0, confirming this 320x ceiling applies to the two in-scope cameras. Conditions[17-20] fix the optical/digital boundary at exactly ZoomPosition==16384 (=0x4000). reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md section 6 supplies the 20 documented optical breakpoints (1x=0x0000 ... 20x=0x4000, non-linear spacing, both P20 and I20 confirmed 20x-lens per their Specifications pages) which my piecewise-linear interpolation reproduces exactly at all 20 breakpoints (worked check in /tmp/edc/reconstruct.py, 'Check C', all OK). No harvested page (grepped reference/crestron-visca for 'digital zoom'/'d.zoom'/'dzoom': zero hits) nor either camera's Specifications page mentions a digital-zoom spec number or its position encoding at all. Separately, tracing the JSON's own control flow (i20.json .Rules[21]: States.ZoomPosition is a literal 16384, NOT the computed {ZoomPositionFromLevel}) proves ZoomLevelToPosition's return value for any ZoomLevel>20 is dead code for absolute 'Set' operations -- the driver clamps 'set a zoom level' requests above 20x to exactly 16384 rather than ever computing a digital-zoom position. By contrast i20.json .Rules[24]/[25] ('SendZoomIn/OutAndZoomStopForZoom Increment/Decrement', Condition 'ZoomPositionIsGreaterThanOrEqualToOpticalZoomMax') show that digital zoom IS reachable, but only via raw pulsed Tele/Wide commands with NO absolute-position math involved -- meaning ZoomPositionToLevel is the only one of the pair that must correctly handle a real device-reported position >16384 (for feedback/polling display), and that segment remains a genuine, functionally-live, unfillable gap.
findings.implication: Ship the interpolated optical-range mapping with confidence bounded to integer-ratio breakpoints (fractional 0.1-step accuracy between them is unverified, only self-consistent by construction); do not attempt to guess the digital-zoom curve for ZoomPositionToLevel without either live device captures at known >20x zoom levels or Crestron documentation this experiment's harvest never surfaced (grepped, absent).

verified.claim: 'ZoomLevelToPosition's output above 20x is provably dead code (Rule 21 always overrides it with a literal 16384), so only ZoomPositionToLevel's digital-range gap is functionally live.'
verified.note: The narrower claim in the evidence paragraph ('dead code for absolute Set operations') is correct and verified (Rules 20/21 are CommandTypes:['Set']; Rule 21's States.ZoomPosition is literally 16384). But the headline claim is broader and does not hold: Rule 22 (ProcessZoomPositionIncrement, CommandTypes:['Increment']) also calls ZoomLevelToPosition, gated only by Conditions[19] ZoomPosition<16384 checked on the PRE-increment position. Near the top of the optical range (e.g. ZoomPosition=16383), the near-saturating curve means the corresponding ZoomLevel is already ~20.0x; adding the 0.1 Step (Rule 22's Sum transformation) can push ZoomLevelAfterPulse fractionally above 20 before ApplyZoomPositionStep ever runs — a live call into the undocumented digital range that is not overridden by any literal fallback the way Rule 21's Set path is. This is reinforced by Rule 26 (FeedbackForZoomLevel, unconditional, AppliesTo ZoomPosition) which keeps the main ZoomLevel controller state synced to ZoomPositionToLevel(ZoomPosition) for the FULL 0-31424 range whenever ZoomPosition changes (including via the raw-pulse digital-zoom path, Rules 24/25) — so ZoomLevel can genuinely hold values >20 and then feed back into a subsequent Increment/Decrement's ZoomLevelToPosition call once position drops back under 16384. So ZoomLevelToPosition's digital-range gap is not purely dead; it has at least one live (if narrow) reachable path, contradicting the 'only ZoomPositionToLevel... is functionally live' framing.

missedOrWrong: The top-level claim/summary 'so only ZoomPositionToLevel's digital-range gap is functionally live' is overstated/refuted — Rule 22 (ProcessZoomPositionIncrement) can call ZoomLevelToPosition with an input fractionally above 20x at the top of the optical range (current ZoomPosition just under 16384 + a 0.1 ZoomLevel.Step), and this is not overridden by any literal fallback the way Rule 21's Set-path is. Rule 26 (FeedbackForZoomLevel, unconditional) further shows the main ZoomLevel controller state is kept synced to ZoomPositionToLevel(ZoomPosition) across the FULL 0-31424 range (not just via 'ReportedZoomLevel'), so a user zooming digitally past 20x via the raw Tele/Wide pulses (Rules 24/25) and then decrementing back down crosses this boundary for real.

The 'second independent confirmation' of ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles via the generalized ViscaAssemble4LowerNibbles / COMMANDS.md '28F6' worked check is presented as an independent doc-stated example but is actually (a) explicitly labeled in COMMANDS.md as a derived/inferred observation, not something Crestron's page states, and (b) circular by construction — the nibble bytes were built by splitting the digits of the very target value being checked, so it doesn't discriminate between candidate implementations the way Check A does. This should be downgraded from 'independent confirmation' to weak corroborating context.

The circumstantial 'Aver AI PTZ VISCA doc snippet' support for FormatRomVersion's dotted-decimal convention has no citable URL and leaves no artifact anywhere under reference/crestron-visca/ (the only permitted write location), violating the project's 'cite a URL/path/offset for every claim — no citation, no finding' rule. It is appropriately hedged as non-probative, but should either have been dropped or given a retrievable citation.

No placeholder or test content was found; all six reconstructions and their confidence ratings are grounded in real, verifiable JSON paths and harvested doc files that I independently reproduced (byte offsets, rule/condition/controller indices, and Reserved-Presets.md/COMMANDS.md/VISCA-Commands.md line content all check out).

analysis.summary: Ran the calibration test first, as instructed. Result: the harvested Crestron VISCA documentation correctly predicts the great majority of the DECLARED (calibration-set) transformation bytes in both drivers — direction codes, on/off codes, exposure-mode codes, the zoom-speed 0-7 nibble range, pan/tilt speed ranges (1-24 / 1-20), the pan/tilt angle*14.4 constant, the CAM_MountMode Stand/Ceiling codes, and the tracking-profile preset numbers 105-108 all match exactly, byte for byte. But the calibration set also contains one clean, reproducible FAILURE: the declared MapIndicatorLightToLedBar transformation sends 0x00 for every 'off' lightbar segment, while the documented Lightbar table requires the off segment to retain its color's 2-bit code (0x01 for red, 0x03 for yellow) even when brightness is off — the driver only agrees with the doc for green (whose off-code is coincidentally 0x00). So documentation earns real but not unconditional trust. Extended to the undeclared holes, that trust cashes out unevenly: the undeclared ViscaExtractNibbles transformation (no driver-local IL; presumably an SDK-framework primitive) behaves exactly as the doc's nibble-packing convention implies (SetFocusPosition/SetZoomPosition match CAM_Focus/CAM_Zoom Direct byte-for-byte). But the undeclared transformations that DO have driver-local IL (FormatRomVersion, ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles) are invoked only against a wholly undocumented c2 09 06/07 'custom inquiry' register block that has zero coverage anywhere in the 16-page doc set — for those specific holes the documentation has nothing to say at all, so the experiment's hoped-for 'fill the precisely-known hole' outcome is simply untestable, not confirmed. Both drivers also reveal a large undocumented vendor-extension command family (autofocus behavior/sensitivity, auto-software-update, group tracking, tracking-framing-profile, 'Identify') riding on the same VISCA c2 envelope Crestron's docs reserve for 'Intelligent Switching' — but at disjoint sub-opcodes, so it's a second, silent extension family layered on top of a documented one, never touched by the driver. The project's standing conclusion — shipped driver bytes are the more trustworthy record when driver and doc disagree — REPRODUCES on the strongest evidence found here (the lightbar off-byte case, and the ZoomPosition range) and is corroborated rather than contradicted overall, but this is the first of the three data points where the documentation also gets a large fraction of the byte-level detail RIGHT, not just wrong.

findings.claim: CALIBRATION largely PASSES: at least 10 independently-checkable declared transformations/ranges match the documented VISCA bytes exactly.
findings.evidence: JSON driver_definition.Transformations (both pkgs) vs reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md: MapBooleanToViscaOnOff true/false -> 0x02/0x03 matches CAM_Power On/Off '04 00 02'/'04 00 03' (COMMANDS.md Sec.4). MapExposureMode true/false -> 0x00/0x03 plus its own comment '...Shutter Priority=0x0a, Iris Priority=0x0b' matches CAM_AE Full Auto/Manual/Shutter/Iris rows exactly. MapFocusDirection Farther/Closer/MapDefault -> 0x02/0x03/0x00 matches CAM_Focus Far/Near(Standard)/Stop. MapZoomSpeedZoomDirection keys '0/In'..'7/In' -> chars 0x20-0x27 and '0/Out'..'7/Out' -> 0x30-0x37 matches CAM_Zoom Tele/Wide(Variable) '2p'/'3p' FF for p=0..7, resolving the doc's own hedge ('p: 0-7 (inferred shared with Tele row above)'). MapPanDirection {Left:1,Right:2,Stop:3} and MapTiltDirection {Up:1,Down:2,Stop:3} exactly decompose every Pan-tiltDrive row (Up '03 01', Down '03 02', Left '01 03', Right '02 03', Stop '03 03'). PanSpeed Controller Min/Max=1/24 and TiltSpeed Min/Max=1/20 match doc's VV 0x01-0x18(24)/WW 0x01-0x14(20) exactly. PanTiltAngleToPosition = Multiply(14.4) and PanAngle/TiltAngle Step=0.069444...(=1/14.4) match the doc's stray, misplaced '1 angle=14.4' fragment (COMMANDS.md Sec.4 note) quantitatively. MapInvertedToHex (P20 only) true/false -> 0x03/0x02 matches CAM_MountMode Ceiling/Stand '04 A4 03'/'04 A4 02' exactly, and this transformation/command pair is absent from the I20 JSON entirely, matching the doc's explicit 'IV-CAM-P12 and IV-CAM-P20 only' scoping. MapTrackingFramingProfileToPreset trackingProfile1-4 -> chars 'i','j','k','l' = 0x69-0x6c = 105-108 decimal, exactly matching Reserved-Presets.md's Tracking Profile 1-4 = presets 105-108. SetFocusPosition/GetFocusPosition Parameters '04 48 Y4 Y3 Y2 Y1'/'04 48' match CAM_Focus Direct/CAM_FocusPosInq '04 48 0p 0q 0r 0s' byte-for-byte via the (undeclared) ViscaExtractNibbles transformation.
findings.implication: The documentation is a genuinely reliable predictor of declared, calibration-set driver behavior for the bulk of the standard VISCA surface (power, zoom/focus/pan-tilt jog & direct positioning, exposure mode, mount mode, tracking-profile preset numbers).

findings.claim: CALIBRATION FAILS on one clean, reproducible case inside the declared set: the lightbar's 'segment off' byte for non-green colors.
findings.evidence: Declared transformation MapIndicatorLightToLedBar (driver_definition.Transformations, Type:'Map') gives 'red/3/Half':'�\r\r�' (bytes 00 0D 0D 00), 'red/2/Half':00 09 09 00, 'red/1/Half':00 05 05 00, 'yellow/3/Half':00 0F 0F 00, 'yellow/2/Half':00 0B 0B 00, 'yellow/1/Half':00 07 07 00 -- i.e. the outer 'off' segments are always 0x00. reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md Sec.8 documents Half Red Bright/Medium/Dim as '01 0D 0D 01'/'01 09 09 01'/'01 05 05 01' and Half Yellow Bright/Medium/Dim as '03 0F 0F 03'/'03 0B 0B 03'/'03 07 07 03' -- outer bytes 0x01 (red) / 0x03 (yellow), not 0x00. Only the Green Half rows happen to match (green's own color code is 0x00, so 'off' and 'off+green' are byte-identical by coincidence). The doc's own worked bit-packing explanation (Sec.1/Sec.8: nibble = brightness(2 bits)<<2 | color(2 bits), color codes green=00/red=01/yellow=11) predicts 0x01 and 0x03 for these off segments, not 0x00.
findings.implication: Documentation does not earn unconditional trust even within the calibration set. Per the project's standing rule (driver bytes are evidence of hardware behavior, doc is evidence of intent), the real device most likely just treats brightness=00 as 'segment off' regardless of the color sub-nibble, making the doc's retained color code functionally moot -- but a system checking exact wire-level conformance against the documented bytes would flag this driver as non-conformant to Crestron's own reference.

findings.claim: One undeclared transformation without driver-local IL (ViscaExtractNibbles) behaves exactly as the doc's nibble convention predicts, extending trust to it despite it having no visible definition in the JSON.
findings.evidence: ViscaExtractNibbles appears 10 times in both driver JSONs' Commands (e.g. SetFocusPosition, SetZoomPosition, SetExposureCompensation, SetPanTiltAngle, SetPtzSuperOperation) but has zero entry in either driver's 26/27-item Transformations array -- it is invoked but not declared, yet unlike FormatRomVersion/ZoomLevelToPosition/etc. it was not named among this camera family's driver-local IL implementations in the task brief, implying it is an SDK-framework primitive shared across Crestron VISCA drivers generically. Its output, when substituted into SetFocusPosition ('04 48 Y4 Y3 Y2 Y1') and SetZoomPosition ('04 47 speed Y4 Y3 Y2 Y1'), reproduces COMMANDS.md's documented CAM_Focus Direct ('04 48 0p 0q 0r 0s') and the corrected reading of CAM_Zoom Direct/Absolute Position exactly.
findings.implication: For holes tied to the standard VISCA nibble-packing idiom, the documentation route genuinely works, extending the experiment's hoped-for result to at least this one undeclared transformation.

findings.claim: The undeclared transformations that DO carry driver-local IL (FormatRomVersion, ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles) are invoked only against a completely undocumented VISCA register block, so the documentation cannot be tested against them at all -- the experiment's key question is untestable for exactly the holes it most wanted to fill.
findings.evidence: driver_definition.Responses[Name=ViscaTrackingFramingProfileInquiryResponse] (I20) matches header 'P' + byte 0x06 + nibble range [0x09-0x0C] + FF and feeds ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles -> Preset -> MapTrackingFramingProfileToPreset; its CommandsProcessed is GetTrackingFramingProfile, itself a ViscaCustomInquiry with Parameters '07' (full packet '8x c2 09 07 FF'). driver_definition.Responses[Name=ViscaVersionInquiryResponse] feeds FormatRomVersion from a 2-byte capture inside the CAM_VersionInq reply. Grepping all 16 harvested doc pages (reference/crestron-visca/*.md) for 'c2 09 07', '0x07' as a custom-inquiry sub-op, or any ROM-version STRING FORMAT description returns nothing -- COMMANDS.md's own Gap #5 already flags this for ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles specifically ('No page in this doc set gives a byte-level definition... by that name or an equivalent').
findings.implication: This is the sharpest finding for the experiment's actual question: documentation cannot fill every precisely-known hole, even when it correctly predicts the calibration set, because some holes sit entirely outside the documented protocol surface (proprietary c2 09 register range) rather than being an undocumented corner of a documented feature.

findings.claim: COVERAGE: both drivers implement a minority of the documented VISCA command-set families, concentrated on power, pan/tilt/zoom/focus positioning and jog, exposure-compensation-only exposure control, presets/reboot/menu/tracking dispatch (via the CAM_Memory-style preset call), and the lightbar -- they ignore White Balance, manual Shutter/Iris/Gain/Bright, Backlight Compensation, IR receiver toggle, Pan-tiltLimitSet, combined CAM_ZoomFocus, and the entire documented 'VISCA Intelligent Switching' 8-command family.
findings.evidence: Enumerated all 82 (I20) / 77 (P20) Commands via pkg_dump.py's driver_definition.Commands. No command anywhere named/parameterized for CAM_WB ('04 35'), CAM_RGain/CAM_BGain ('04 03'/'04 43'/'04 04'/'04 44'), CAM_Shutter/CAM_Iris/CAM_Gain/CAM_Bright ('04 0A'/'04 4A' etc.), CAM_Backlight ('04 33'), IR_Receive ('06 08'), Pan-tiltLimitSet ('06 07'), CAM_ZoomFocus combined Direct, or any of the eight VISCA Intelligent Switching commands (Set/Get Camera, Clear All Cameras, Call Camera Output, Resume/Pause Intelligent Switching, Get Output, Check Connection Status -- all documented in reference/crestron-visca/VISCA-Intelligent-Switching-Commands.md and tabulated in COMMANDS.md Sec.9) appears in either driver's Commands array.
findings.implication: The 1 Beyond control-system driver is a deliberately narrow subset of the full VISCA surface Crestron documents for these cameras -- consistent with an AV-control integrator only needing PTZ + basic exposure + presets + status LED, not full imaging fine-tuning or multi-camera VISCA-level switching (multi-camera switching is presumably handled by Crestron's own separate application layer, not this per-camera IP driver).

findings.claim: EXTRAS: both drivers implement Privacy Mode entirely via a mechanical pan/tilt trick (drive to TiltAngle.Max/Min), not any VISCA privacy register -- and the documentation's own privacy-mode gate ('cameras cannot use VISCA commands in Privacy Mode... send the wake command first') never gives a command for entering/exiting that mode.
findings.evidence: driver_definition.Commands[Name=PrivacyCommand] Info.CommandName='SetPanTiltAngle' with Values {PanSpeed:'{PanSpeed.Max}', TiltSpeed:'{TiltSpeed.Max}', PanAngle:'{PanAngle}'}; EnablePrivacy sets TiltAngle to '{TiltAngle.Max}', DisablePrivacy to '{TiltAngleDisablePrivacy}' (P20 additionally has EnablePrivacyInverted using '{TiltAngle.Min}' for ceiling-mounted units). This resolves to the ordinary Pan-tiltDrive Absolute Position VISCA command ('01 06 02 ...'), not any dedicated privacy opcode. reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md's own 'Gaps' section (#1) independently flags that no VISCA-Commands page anywhere in this doc set gives a byte sequence for a 'wake' command despite the page's prose requiring one.
findings.implication: 'Privacy Mode' as the doc describes it (an internal camera state that blocks VISCA commands) and 'Privacy' as the driver implements it (physically tilting the lens out of view) may be two different mechanisms achieving a similar visual effect -- the driver substitutes a mechanical workaround precisely where the documentation is silent on the real protocol-level command, echoing (but not identically reproducing) the Automate VX Wake/Sleep asymmetry from findings/08: there, the driver called an undocumented Wake; here, neither the driver nor the doc has anything resembling one, and the driver instead avoids needing Wake/Sleep-Privacy VISCA opcodes altogether.

findings.claim: EXTRAS: both drivers define an undocumented family of 'custom' VISCA commands (autofocus behavior/sensitivity, auto-software-update, group tracking, tracking-framing-profile, 'Identify') using the SAME c2-prefixed VISCA envelope the documentation reserves for 'Intelligent Switching', but at disjoint sub-opcodes never mentioned in any harvested page.
findings.evidence: driver_definition.Commands[Name=ViscaCustomCommand/ViscaCustomInquiry] resolve to Message 'c2 01 {Parameters}' / 'c2 09 {Parameters}'. Concrete sub-opcodes used: GetAutoFocusBehavior/SetAutoFocusBehavior='02', GetAutoFocusSensitivity/SetAutoFocusSensitivity='03', GetAutoSoftwareUpdate/SetAutoSoftwareUpdate='04', GetGroupTracking='06', GetTrackingFramingProfile='07' (I20 only), Identify='01 0a'. reference/crestron-visca/VISCA-Intelligent-Switching-Commands.md and COMMANDS.md Sec.9 document c2 01/09 sub-opcodes 08 (Call Camera Output / Get Output), 09 (Set/Get Camera IP), 0A (Clear All Cameras), 0B (Pause Intelligent Switching), 0d (Check Connection Status) -- none overlap with 01-07.
findings.implication: Crestron/1 Beyond appear to have carved the vendor-extension VISCA command-type byte (0xC2) into (at least) two disjoint sub-ranges for two unrelated feature sets -- one documented (multi-camera Intelligent Switching), one entirely undocumented (per-camera AI/tracking tuning) -- and the driver only ever uses the undocumented half. This is the clearest 'vendor-specific extension the docs are silent on' finding of the three data points collected so far in this project.

findings.claim: CONTRADICTION candidate: the driver's real addressable ZoomPosition range (0-31424) is roughly 1.92x the documented 20x-zoom lookup table's endpoint (0-16384 / 0x4000).
findings.evidence: driver_definition.Controllers[Name=ZoomPosition].Info = {Mode:'AbsoluteRange', Min:0, Max:31424} identically in both i20.json and p20.json. reference/crestron-visca/COMMANDS.md Sec.6 20x Zoom table runs '1x'->0000 through '20x'->4000 (16384 decimal), and both P20 and I20 spec pages (IV-CAM-P20-Specifications.md, IV-CAM-I20-Specifications.md) state '20x' optical zoom, so the 20x table is the applicable one per the doc's own text.
findings.implication: Either the camera has meaningful digital-zoom headroom past its documented optical-zoom position table (which the doc's Zoom Ratio/Position table never mentions), or the doc's table only covers part of the addressable value space. Either way the driver's own declared attribute range carries information the documentation does not state anywhere; flagged as medium confidence because the FieldOfView Controller elsewhere in the same JSON uses Min/Max=0/16384 (matching the doc), so the JSON itself is not fully self-consistent about what the 'true' zoom-position ceiling is.

findings.claim: I20 vs P20: most of the command-set delta between the two drivers IS explained by the documentation's own model-scoping language, with one probable but not certain naming exception.
findings.evidence: I20-only commands GetTrackingFraming/StartTrackingFraming/StopTrackingFraming/GetGroupTracking/EnableGroupTracking/GetTrackingFramingProfile/SetTrackingFramingProfile map to VISCA bytes ('08 01' inquiry; presets 0x50/0x51/0x52 = 80/81/82) that Reserved-Presets.md explicitly scopes to 'IV-CAM-I12, IV-CAM-I20...' or 'IV-CAM-I20' only, and CAM_TrackingInq ('09 08 01') is a real documented inquiry. P20-only GetInverted/SetInverted (preset-independent, '04 A4') match CAM_MountMode, explicitly scoped by COMMANDS.md to 'IV-CAM-P12 and IV-CAM-P20 only'. The one loose end: the driver's 'EnablePresenterTracking' command sends preset 0x53 (83 decimal), but Reserved-Presets.md's table labels preset 83 'Pause Group Tracking' (IV-CAM-I20), not 'Enable Presenter Tracking' -- resolved plausibly, not conclusively, by that same doc page's own prose ('Preset 80 starts the camera's respective intelligent function (Group Framing or Presenter Tracking)... an IV-CAM-I20... camera can start (82) or pause (83) Group Tracking'), i.e. pausing the forced Group-Tracking mode may functionally fall back to the camera's other configured intelligent function (Presenter Tracking), making the driver's command name a description of the resulting behavior rather than of the literal preset function name.
findings.implication: Dimension 4's answer is mostly 'documentation explains the split' (tracking hardware only on I-series, mount-mode only on P-series), with one command-naming discrepancy that is more likely an interpretation gap in the doc's own preset table than a real driver bug, given the doc's own text about mutual exclusivity of the two intelligent functions.

openQuestions: Does the actual 1 Beyond hardware visually/functionally distinguish lightbar segments that are 'off+red' (0x01) from 'off+yellow' (0x03) from 'off+green' (0x00) -- i.e. is the calibration-set lightbar mismatch truly harmless, or does Crestron's own doc encode a real hardware distinction the driver is silently getting wrong?

What does the camera actually do with ZoomPosition values between 16384 and 31424 -- is that a documented-but-unlabeled digital zoom range, or does the 20x Zoom table the docs give simply not cover the device's full addressable range?
Is there a P20-equivalent of the I20's undocumented c2 09 06/07 tracking registers, or are those genuinely I20-only vendor extensions with no P20 analog to compare against?

Was 'EnablePresenterTracking' -> preset 0x53 verified against real hardware behavior anywhere in this project's other notes, or is the 'pause Group Tracking falls back to Presenter Tracking' reading purely inferred from the Reserved-Presets prose?

verified.claim: Calibration PASSES on >=10 declared transformations/ranges: MapBooleanToViscaOnOff 0x02/0x03, MapExposureMode 0x00/0x03 (+comment 0x0a/0x0b), MapFocusDirection 0x02/0x03/0x00, MapZoomSpeedZoomDirection 0x20-0x27/0x30-0x37, MapPanDirection/MapTiltDirection {1,2,3}, PanSpeed 1-24/TiltSpeed 1-20, PanTiltAngleToPosition x14.4 (and inverse 1/14.4 step), MapInvertedToHex 0x03/0x02 (P20-only, absent from I20), MapTrackingFramingProfileToPreset 105-108 (I20-only, absent from P20).
verified.note: Reproduced every one of these directly against pkg_dump output for both pkgs and against COMMANDS.md/Reserved-Presets.md. Byte values, ranges, and model-scoping (P20-only MapInvertedToHex, I20-only MapTrackingFramingProfileToPreset) all match exactly as claimed.

verified.claim: MapIndicatorLightToLedBar (declared) disagrees with the documented Lightbar table: driver sends 0x00 for the outer 'off' segment on red/yellow Half combinations, while COMMANDS.md/VISCA-Lightbar-Commands.md document 0x01 (red) / 0x03 (yellow) for those same outer bytes; only Green (whose own color code is 0x00) coincides.
verified.note: Reproduced exact bytes both sides: driver red/3/Half=00 0D 0D 00, doc Half Red Bright=01 0D 0D 01; driver yellow/3/Half=00 0F 0F 00, doc Half Yellow Bright=03 0F 0F 03. This is a real, clean calibration-set failure exactly as described.

verified.claim: ViscaExtractNibbles is invoked (10x in each driver JSON) but not declared in either Transformations array, and its use in SetFocusPosition/SetZoomPosition reproduces the documented CAM_Focus Direct / CAM_Zoom Direct nibble-packed byte patterns.
verified.note: Confirmed the invocation count (10 in each JSON) and the absent declaration, and confirmed the template shapes '04 48 {Y4}{Y3}{Y2}{Y1}' / '04 47 {speed}{Y4}{Y3}{Y2}{Y1}' match the doc's '04 48 0p 0q 0r 0s' / '04 47 0p 0q 0r 0s' pattern structurally. But 'reproduces ... byte-for-byte' overclaims: the JSON alone cannot establish which nibble (Y4 or Y1) is most-significant, so an alternative nibble-order implementation is equally consistent with the same evidence -- this is a genuine reconstruction ambiguity the finding does not flag.

verified.claim: The undeclared, driver-local-IL transformations FormatRomVersion and ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles are both invoked only against a wholly undocumented c2 09 06/07 custom-inquiry register block with zero coverage anywhere in the doc set, making the documentation route untestable for exactly these holes.
verified.note: Half of this claim is wrong by the researcher's own cited evidence. ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles is indeed invoked only via GetTrackingFramingProfile -> 'c2 09 07' (undocumented, confirmed). But FormatRomVersion is invoked on ViscaVersionInquiryResponse, which processes GetDeviceInformation -- and GetDeviceInformation resolves to ViscaInquiry Parameters '00 02', i.e. the full packet '8x 09 00 02 FF', which is exactly Crestron's documented CAM_VersionInq (COMMANDS.md line 269: '8x 09 00 02 FF' / reply 'y0 50 00 01 mn pq rs tu vw FF -- r,s,t,u: ROM version'). This is the DOCUMENTED command family (09 xx), not the undocumented c2 09 block. The doc even gives the byte position of the 2-byte ROM version field, matching the JSON's 2-byte regex capture exactly. The researcher's own evidence sentence ('FormatRomVersion feeds from a 2-byte capture inside the CAM_VersionInq reply') already states this, directly contradicting their claim's framing. What is genuinely undocumented is only the narrower question of how those 2 raw bytes get formatted into a human-readable version string -- not 'the whole register' or 'zero coverage'. This finding, which the report explicitly calls 'the sharpest finding for the experiment's actual question,' is overstated to the point of being wrong for the FormatRomVersion half.

verified.claim: COVERAGE: both drivers implement only a subset of documented VISCA families, and ignore White Balance, manual Shutter/Iris/Gain/Bright, Backlight Compensation, IR receiver toggle, Pan-tiltLimitSet, combined CAM_ZoomFocus, and the 8-command VISCA Intelligent Switching family.
verified.note: Enumerated all 82 (I20) / 77 (P20) driver Commands (counts match exactly) and confirmed none of these documented families appear. Also confirmed the Intelligent Switching family is exactly 8 documented commands (Set Camera, Get Camera, Clear All Cameras, Call Camera Output, Resume, Pause, Get Output, Check Connection Status).

verified.claim: EXTRAS: Privacy Mode is implemented entirely via a mechanical pan/tilt trick (SetPanTiltAngle to TiltAngle.Max/Min), not any VISCA privacy register; the doc likewise never gives a byte sequence for entering/exiting Privacy Mode (only the 'Wake' gate prose, per Gap #1).
verified.note: The mechanical PrivacyCommand/EnablePrivacy/DisablePrivacy(/EnablePrivacyInverted on P20) mechanism and the doc's Gap #1 (no Wake byte sequence) are both confirmed exactly as described. But 'entirely ... not any VISCA privacy register' is too strong: both drivers also define GetAutoPrivacyMode/SetAutoPrivacyMode, an actual VISCA-addressed register ('0e 24 26 00 {OnOff}') that is privacy-related and also undocumented anywhere in the harvested pages. The researcher's own claim list never mentions this command at all, so the 'entirely mechanical, no VISCA privacy register' framing is contradicted by evidence sitting right next to what they did cite (PrivacyCommand) in the same Commands array.

verified.claim: EXTRAS: both drivers use undocumented c2 01/c2 09 sub-opcodes (02,03,04,06,07, plus '01 0a' for Identify) for AI/tracking-tuning commands, disjoint from the documented Intelligent Switching sub-opcodes (08,09,0A,0B,0d) that ride the same c2 tag byte.
verified.note: Reproduced every cited sub-opcode exactly (GetAutoFocusBehavior/SetAutoFocusBehavior='02', AutoFocusSensitivity='03', AutoSoftwareUpdate='04', GroupTracking='06', TrackingFramingProfile='07', Identify='01 0a') against pkg_dump output, and confirmed VISCA-Intelligent-Switching-Commands.md's documented sub-opcodes (09,0A,08,0B,0d) do not overlap with the driver's used range.

verified.claim: CONTRADICTION candidate: ZoomPosition Controller range (0-31424) is ~1.92x the documented 20x-zoom table's 0-16384 endpoint, while the FieldOfView Controller in the same JSON uses 0-16384 (matching the doc) -- an internal inconsistency in the driver's own declared ranges.
verified.note: Reproduced both Controller Info blocks exactly (ZoomPosition Min/Max 0/31424; FieldOfView Min/Max 0/16384) and confirmed the doc's 20x zoom table runs 0000-4000 (0-16384) as claimed. However, the researcher missed a much stronger, more directly-worded piece of corroborating evidence for the same underlying fact sitting in the very same Controllers array: a 'ZoomLevel' Controller with Min=1.0, Max=320.0 (i.e. up to 32.0x in 0.1 units), directly contradicting the Specifications pages' explicit '20x Optical Zoom' figure that the researcher already cites elsewhere in the same report -- this would have upgraded this finding from medium to high confidence had it been found.

verified.claim: I20 vs P20: the command-set split (tracking commands I20-only, MountMode/Inverted P20-only) is explained by the doc's own model-scoping language, with one loose naming end (EnablePresenterTracking -> preset 0x53=83, but Reserved-Presets.md labels 83 'Pause Group Tracking' not 'Enable Presenter Tracking').

Reproduced the EnablePresenterTracking->Preset 0x53(83) discrepancy against Reserved-Presets.md's table row '83 | Pause Group Tracking | IV-CAM-I20' exactly; the researcher appropriately hedged this as medium confidence and speculative rather than overclaiming a resolution.
